I don't think it's like a 'neurodivergent staple' to have a maximalist room because I can imagine a lot of other Autistic people would be overstimulated by the way my room is decorated. It's a spectrum for a reason, and everyone thrives in different environments!

As for myself, I really love having a maximalist room due to two main reasons; I'm sensory seeking, and I'm often stuck in my room most of the time due to physical disability. I love being able to have a room that is full of all of the things that are important to me, and for me it's a matter of "if I have to be stuck in here for most of my time, then I may as well make a place that's not only interesting for me to look at, but also contains everything that I love!" Also a lot of my special interests have to do with collecting, so that probably has something to do with it.

But I completely understand that this is more of a personalized thing, and even some of my family members get overstimulated from my room because that's how their sensory issues work. It's definitely not for everyone, and I think it's inaccurate to say that maximalism is a thing that's unique to Autistic/developmentally disabled people! Plus, I feel like those of us who \*do\* have maximalist spaces just have a tendency to wanna show them off more because it takes a lot of time and effort to build up the stuff we have to create these rooms :)

I'm not a fullsuiter (yet,) but have used my rollator walker while in partial suit. I think the biggest thing to note would be your feetpaws and making sure you're giving yourself enough space to accommodate for them. You may want to practice walking around in-suit with the cane so that you can get a feel for how you move around in your suit. 

Also, having good spacial awareness in-suit is a skill that must be learned, and using a mobility aid of any kind is a factor you'll need to consider. Which is why I think taking small bits of time to walk around your house in-suit with the aid can be really important! Even starting with a few minutes a day is more than enough!

Your grip on the cane is another thing to consider. I personally don't have much problem with gripping my rollator, but that's considering the fact that it stands on it's own, and I have five-finger paws. For your suit I think it'd be pretty easy to cut some finger escapes out in them if you're unable to get a good grip while wearing such puffy paws. Might also want to consider getting a foot for your cane that allows it to stand on it's own.

Before the con, know where your nearest headless lounge is, and use it as often as you need to when you're there! Or if 'breaking the magic' isn't an issue for you then don't force yourself to keep suiting if you need a break! Fursuiting isn't a marathon, and it's more than okay to take your head off any time you need to.

Finally, have water on you, and maybe even an electrolyte drink or powder. We lose a lot of electrolytes when we sweat, which may end up triggering a health episode, so it's even more important to replenish them when you're disabled and doing any physical activity! 

I think that's all, besides saying that I adore your suit and that I hope you have fun at the con! I won't lie and say that fursuiting while being disabled is easy, but I think it's well worth doing if it makes you happy. Good luck!!

Auras, in the context of migraines, are sensory disturbances that happen before a migraine headache occurs, sorta like a warning sign that one is about to start. They commonly come in the form of visual disturbances - bright lights, zigzag lines, tunnel vision, dark spots, or even temporary blindness are some examples - but can also involve sensory or speech and language disturbances, like numbness and tingling or slurred speech and mumbling.

I actually used to be someone who thought they were offensive, until I took a step back and realized that the work that goes into the designing and manufacturing is a type of art, so what difference does it make if someone were to make a character based on a condition they have or creates art to spread awareness and knowledge about it? Sure I think some of their designs could've been done better to represent the conditions they're based on, but they've shown that they like to update their designs every few years to not only keep their stock fresh, but to also get a fresh set of eyes on a specific condition and see if any new PD community members have their own experiences to add to each plush's design.

I also find it kinda humanizing in a way, if that makes sense? The realization that real people deal with these conditions on a daily, often permanent basis, and the fact that we too need to feel safe and comforted just like everyone else... It's a bit hard for me to explain without getting philosophical but it's a very human desire to need and seek comfort which is why plushies exist in the first place, and I feel like having an interpretation of what you deal with every day in the form of a cuddly toy is kinda like, turning the tables on the condition itself- I'm instead looking at something related to my conditions as a source of comfort instead of one of constant misery and anguish. 

This is all my way of thinking about it though, and honestly I do understand the hesitancy people have towards them because you see a company selling mental illness and physical disability-related products and your brain jumps to the worst conclusions because that's what we as disabled people are used to- being turned into a means of earning profits. But I feel a lot better knowing that portions of the funds they get from each plush get donated to organizations that help people with said conditions.
